title: Fairy-Tale Castles
objective: After this level you can describe Neuschwanstein and other romantic castles.
summary: Neuschwanstein (begun 1869 for Ludwig II) copies no real castle: stage-set designs mixing old motifs. Behind the knightly look: brick, steel, central heating, telephones.

cards.headline: The world's most famous 'medieval' castle had telephones.
cards.body: Neuschwanstein, in Bavaria, was begun in 1869 for King Ludwig II, who built it to withdraw from public life. It was still unfinished when he died in 1886, and within weeks it opened to the public. So is it a castle at all?

cards.headline: A castle from a stage set
cards.body: Ludwig wrote to Richard Wagner, whom he greatly admired, that he would build 'in the authentic style of the old German knights' castles'. The designs came from stage sets by the Munich scene painter Christian Jank, turned into plans by the architect Eduard Riedel. Neuschwanstein copies no real building. It mixes motifs from the Wartburg castle with castles from medieval book illustrations, a style called historicism.

cards.headline: Why a king built a dream
cards.body: In 1866 Bavaria lost a war to Prussia, and Ludwig was no longer a sovereign ruler. From 1867 he planned his own kingdom instead, in castles and palaces where he could be a real king. Romantic castles ran in the family: his father, Maximilian II, had rebuilt the nearby ruin of Hohenschwangau in a 'Gothic style' from 1832.

cards.fact: Medieval on the outside, modern inside.
cards.context: The walls are brick, with pale limestone only as a skin. The Throne Hall is an encased steel construction: Level 8's metal, hidden inside a 'Romanesque' hall. Inside there was hot-air central heating, running water on every floor, toilets that flushed automatically, electric bells to call servants and telephones on two floors.

learned: Begun 1869 for Ludwig II, as a retreat

questions.prompt: Which of these did Neuschwanstein have behind its medieval look?

options.label: A moat and a working drawbridge
options.rationale: Its surprises were modern, not medieval.

options.label: Murder holes over every gateway
options.rationale: It was built as a retreat, not a fortress.

options.label: Walls of solid carved limestone
options.rationale: The walls are brick, with limestone only as cladding.

questions.explanation: Neuschwanstein had hot-air central heating, running water on every floor, automatic flushing toilets, electric bells and telephones.

questions.prompt: Why is Neuschwanstein called historicism rather than a real medieval castle?

options.label: It is a stone-by-stone copy of the Wartburg castle
It was built in the Middle Ages and later restored
It is a ruin that has stood untouched since 1500
It copies no real castle, mixing old motifs anew

questions.explanation: Neuschwanstein copies no existing building; it combines motifs from the Wartburg with castles from medieval book illustrations.

questions.prompt: Neuschwanstein's Throne Hall is a steel construction. What does steel offer that Level 8 said stone and cast iron lack?

options.label: High tensile strength: it resists stretching
A lower price than any stone
options.rationale: The point is strength, not price.

options.label: The ability to heal its own cracks

questions.explanation: Steel has high tensile strength, while stone and cast iron are weak when stretched.
